detections.evidence_quote: when I worked in London, people used to call in hungover
detections.summary: Speakers riff on the cultural contrast between British and American attitudes toward calling in hungover.

detections.evidence_quote: There's been various attempts to like create antioxidants in a lab and turn them into vitamin supplements. There's no evidence that they do anything.
detections.summary: Speaker debunks lab-synthesized antioxidant vitamin supplements, saying there is no evidence they do anything.

detections.evidence_quote: Okay, the next sort of debunkery is the antioxidants stuff.
detections.summary: Speaker explicitly frames the antioxidant supplement claim as the next item of 'debunkery'.

detections.evidence_quote: all of the studies on resveratrol, since the 1990s have found, you don't really absorb it, you get a spike of it for roughly 30 minutes
detections.summary: Speaker explains that resveratrol is poorly absorbed, briefly spikes, and is broken down before it can provide benefit.

detections.evidence_quote: all of the studies on resveratrol, since the 1990s have found
detections.summary: Speaker cites the body of resveratrol studies since the 1990s to support the absorption claim.

detections.evidence_quote: the only real evidence that resveratrol could be isolated and could have these health effects is on studies of yeast, fruit flies and mice
detections.summary: Speaker notes resveratrol's health effects are only shown in yeast, fruit fly, and high-dose mouse studies equivalent to 100 liters of wine.

detections.evidence_quote: the only real evidence that resveratrol could be isolated and could have these health effects is on studies of yeast, fruit flies and mice
detections.summary: Speaker points out that resveratrol's evidence base is limited to yeast, fruit fly, and mouse studies.

detections.evidence_quote: He found that grape juice had more of the heart protecting chemical than 60% of the wines he analyzed.
detections.summary: A 1992 New York Times article quoting a Cornell researcher found grape juice had more of the 'heart protecting chemical' than most wines tested.

detections.evidence_quote: reported Dr. Leroy Creasy, a specialist in fruit cultivation at Cornell University.
detections.summary: The quoted finding is attributed to a named fruit cultivation specialist at Cornell University.

detections.evidence_quote: I think drinking red wine is totally legitimate.
detections.summary: Speaker argues the resveratrol/French paradox narrative mainly served as permission to drink red wine, which he considers fine in itself.

detections.evidence_quote: It is the ultimate claim of any diet, which is you can eat whatever you want and still lose weight.
detections.summary: Speaker likens the French paradox to the ultimate diet claim that you can eat whatever you want and still lose weight.

detections.evidence_quote: there is very good evidence that not drinking is the healthiest way to live. And there is very good evidence that moderate drinking is the healthiest way to live.
detections.summary: Speaker summarizes a meta-analysis finding both abstaining and moderate drinking are supported as healthy options, with individual advice to do what works for you.

detections.evidence_quote: I read a really interesting meta-analysis of what we know about mortality, and alcohol and J-shaped and all this kind of stuff.
detections.summary: Speaker cites reading a meta-analysis on mortality and alcohol as the basis for the claims that follow.

detections.evidence_quote: French people have low heart attack rates.
detections.summary: Speaker begins to critique the French paradox by naming the premise that French people have low heart attack rates.
